candidateRows: Theism readily grounds ordinary morality, whereas radically redefining morality does not provide a genuine moral foundation.
This establishes David's thesis and specifies the obligations, values, responsibility, and improvement that a successful foundation must explain.
At the outset of his case, David identifies the debate's scope, states the comparative thesis, and defines the moral phenomena he says require grounding.
Consistent skepticism permits accepting both God and objective morality or rejecting both, but not rejecting God while retaining objective morality without comparable support.
The skeptic's dilemma supplies a principal epistemic argument against non-theistic moral realism and links the standards for God and objective morality.
After comparing unsupported religious and moral intuitions, David formalizes his claim that the same evidential standard should govern theism and objective moral facts.
On atheism, evolutionary hardwiring and social conditioning explain moral beliefs without making them true, thereby undermining trust in moral cognition.
This is David's main debunking argument that a non-theistic universe lacks moral facts and leaves human moral faculties systematically unreliable.
David describes humans as products of purposeless natural processes and argues that survival pressures or social conditioning cannot generate genuine moral facts.
Theism explains objective moral properties and human access to them because God can ground goodness and possess authority to impose universal obligations.
It directly supplies the affirmative foundation the motion asks for, complementing David's critique of secular and atheistic alternatives.
David argues both from a theistic hypothesis to expected moral experience and backward from nonphysical moral properties and universal authority to God.
God is a proposed entity rather than an ethical system, while secular humanism is an articulated method for improving human life.
This challenges whether abstract theism is even a comparable moral foundation and states secular humanism's practical principles and evaluative focus.
David's opening treats theism or God as a moral foundation superior to secular humanism.
Matt disputes the comparison between a proposed deity and an ethical philosophy, emphasizing religious disagreement and secular humanism's human-centered principles.
Morality need not be an intrinsic objective imperative because people who care about flourishing can assess actions by their consequences for shared life.
It presents Matt's core account of how conditional shared concern for well-being can support practical moral assessment without objective intrinsic values.
David's claim that morality ordinarily requires objective values and obligations grounded beyond human attitudes.
Matt denies that the universe commands concern for well-being but argues that actual shared concern permits cooperative evaluation of actions and consequences.
Like chess, shared human goals can generate non-subjective judgments about better and worse actions because physical consequences constrain available choices.
The analogy explains how objective assessments can follow from chosen goals and real-world facts even when the foundational rules or values are not intrinsic.
David's contention that secular moral judgments lack a defensible objective foundation or evidential basis.
Matt compares moral deliberation to evaluating chess moves, then grounds better and worse life choices in physical facts, survival, and reasoned resolution of disagreements.
Secular humanism offers explicit, revisable principles for human flourishing, whereas abstract God claims are disputed, unverifiable, and too unstable to guide improvement.
It gives Matt's fullest direct comparison: an empirical and adaptable human-centered system against an unclear deity whose existence, aims, and instructions remain contested.
David's assertion that theism supplies a better foundation while secular humanism cannot adequately account for morality.
Matt invokes secular-humanist manifesto principles, adaptability, cooperation, and human benefit, then contrasts them with disagreement over God and allegedly anti-flourishing religious models.
God is not merely an unspecified being but the creator, sustainer, and ultimate ground whose image in humans makes moral values and obligations correspond to reality.
This directly repairs the affirmative foundation against Matt's claim that God is only a proposed entity and cannot constitute a moral system.
Matt's argument that God is merely a proposed entity rather than a philosophy, system, or usable moral foundation.
David answers Matt by specifying the morally relevant divine attributes and arguing that creation in God's image supports real rights, values, and obligations.
A goal-dependent well-being system cannot impose obligations on dissenters and can validate horrific means toward immoral goals, so it mutilates rather than grounds morality.
The argument targets the operative mechanism of Matt's secular account, alleging that optional goals eliminate universal duties and permit atrocities under alternative objectives.
Matt's claim that people sharing a concern for well-being can derive better and worse actions while excluding those who reject the goal.
David accepts that agreed goals permit instrumental rules but argues that Matt's account leaves nonparticipants without duties and turns any chosen end into a source of purported obligations.
A moral foundation cannot plausibly rest on a general human tendency to seek others' well-being because history displays pervasive mass atrocities.
The argument directly challenges the secular account's claimed motivational basis by invoking large-scale historical counterexamples to general concern for human welfare.
Matt's claim that people generally care about survival, flourishing, and a better shared life.
At the end of his rebuttal, Wood turns from conditional obligation to historical evidence and argues that twentieth-century atrocities undermine reliance on widespread concern for human well-being.
Being alive places people in the consequential game of life, while invoking God neither motivates the wholly indifferent person nor prevents religiously justified atrocities.
This move defends the secular analogy at the heart of Dillahunty's case while directly denying that the proposed theistic foundation solves motivation or atrocity problems.
Wood's objections that secular obligations depend on voluntarily chosen goals and that historical atrocities discredit human-centered ethics.

Dillahunty clarifies that chess represents unavoidable participation in life, argues that practical consequences can be assessed without God, and answers Wood's Nazi example by noting that divine appeals can authorize atrocities.
Secular humanism offers goals and methods for correcting moral disagreement, whereas merely positing a creator does not establish that creator's goodness, commands, or authority.
The passage supplies a comparative case for secular humanism and attacks the inferential gap between a creator's existence and a usable, justified foundation for ethics.
Wood's contention that a creator God can ground objective duties while secular humanism lacks a sufficient moral foundation.

Dillahunty argues that most people seek improved lives, that secular humanism can investigate consequences and resolve disagreements, and that creator language supplies neither moral character nor justified obligations.
Milgram-style obedience findings and recurrent historical atrocities cast doubt on building ethics from the claim that ordinary people seek others' well-being.
The move introduces empirical evidence intended to undercut the reliability of the secular framework's asserted human motivation and therefore its adequacy as an ethical foundation.
Matt's rebuttal claim that the overwhelming majority generally want survival, better lives, and improved outcomes for society.

Wood cites obedience experiments and mass violence to argue that average people readily harm others under authority, then asks how much ethical weight can rest on an assumed concern for general well-being.
Secular humanism can use knowledge of conformity and manipulation to promote doing good for reciprocal human benefit without relying on divine commands.
This is an affirmative comparative defense explaining how secular humanism incorporates evidence about human weakness and supplies a non-theistic reason for prosocial conduct.
Wood's use of obedience experiments and atrocities to argue that human concern for well-being is too weak to ground ethics.

Dillahunty treats conformity research as information a self-correcting secular system can use, arguing that people should help others because interconnected benefits raise outcomes for everyone rather than because God commands it.
Agreement on seeking well-being cannot ground ethics because radically harmful movements can sincerely describe their incompatible programs as paths to well-being.
The argument targets the secular framework's proposed goal itself, claiming that shared well-being language radically underdetermines conduct and can accompany disastrous policies.
Matt's claim that secular humanism can orient conduct toward a better world and correct harmful behavior through evidence and education.
Wood argues that Nazis, communists, and misguided reformers may all claim to pursue well-being, so widespread verbal agreement on the goal can still yield incompatible and catastrophic results.
People can be mistaken about what improves the world, but shared commitment to improvement permits evidence and internal consistency to expose harmful means as self-defeating.
This response distinguishes fallibility about means from commitment to an ethical end and explains how the secular framework can criticize purported well-being programs from within.
Wood's argument that Nazis and other destructive movements could all profess to seek well-being while producing radically different outcomes.

Dillahunty says harmful programs may pay lip service to well-being while conflicting with their stated end; evidence can reveal the conflict and rationally require revision of either the means or the professed goal.
On the secular account, moral obligations become unreal unless a person adopts the goal of human well-being, leaving the unwilling person without genuine duties.
This formulates the core theistic objection that instrumental rules conditional on a goal cannot provide genuine moral obligation to someone who rejects that goal.
Matt's distinction between atheism and secular humanism and his claim that participation in social life generates assessable consequences.

Wood clarifies that he is not claiming atheism directly causes violence; he argues instead that atheism makes apparently real duties delusional and that Dillahunty's rules apply only after adopting welfare as a goal.
Physical consequences and social interdependence make some ways of living better than others, so discouraging violence needs no intrinsic universal moral imposition.
The move presents the central naturalistic grounding: objective facts about consequences support social norms and better outcomes without requiring an externally imposed divine imperative.
Wood's demand for a genuine moral obligation beyond agreed game rules and his claim that rejecting well-being eliminates secular duties.

Dillahunty argues that life's physical rules determine the effects of violence on victims, offenders, and society; broader attention to those effects supports discouraging murder and improving the world without divine authority.
People unavoidably participate in social life, and objective facts can identify better worlds even when individuals reject the goal or lack motivation to meet reciprocal obligations.
The passage directly addresses the conditionality objection by locating obligation in unavoidable circumstances, factual consequences, shared benefits, and the community's defined moral standards.
Wood's characterization of Dillahunty's moral obligations as conditional on first agreeing to seek human well-being.

Dillahunty distinguishes voluntary agreement from unavoidable participation in life, argues that physical facts make some worlds superior independently of opinion, and grounds reciprocal obligation in benefits already received from society.
Secular humanism cannot supply a moral obligation for someone who does not care about human well-being or flourishing.
The challenge targets whether secular humanism can generate obligations rather than merely identify effective means after a goal has been accepted.
Dillahunty's claim that social circumstances and physical facts impose obligations connected to well-being.
Wood distinguishes conditional guidance toward an accepted goal from an obligation binding a person who rejects the goal and asks why an indifferent universe favors humans over viruses.
Physical facts need not care about humanity to show that opposing threats to human flourishing serves humanist morality.
The answer explains how descriptive facts can guide human-centered moral action without attributing preferences, purposes, or concern to the universe itself.
Wood's objection that the universe does not care whether coronavirus or humanity flourishes.
Dillahunty agrees that the universe is indifferent but argues that facts about a virus harming humans give a humanist reason to oppose it because morality concerns human conduct and interests.
Secular humanism offers a more resilient moral motivation by appealing to evidence and consequences rather than unverifiable divine rewards or threats.
The argument directly compares the proposed foundations and claims that evidence-based humanist motivation survives changes in theology whereas God-based motivation may collapse with belief.
Wood's claim that people require conditioning into concern beyond their limited personal flourishing.

Dillahunty says both religious and secular systems can motivate people, but religion can motivate through false claims, while secular humanism appeals to observable consequences and remains applicable whether or not a god exists.
Theism grounds human worth, objective moral standards, and trustworthy moral cognition in creation by God, unlike an atheistic account of evolved attitudes.
This is Wood's extended positive account of how God purportedly supplies objective value, obligation, human rights, and a basis for trusting moral experience.
Dillahunty's demand that Wood solve the stated problem of moral obligation by appealing to God.

Wood contrasts viewing a person as an accidental organism with viewing that person as God's image-bearer, then argues that a creator can establish goodness and design human faculties to apprehend moral truths.
Appealing to God's image does not itself derive a prohibition on killing, and scriptural commands to kill expose the dependence on further human interpretation.
The exchange attacks the alleged derivation of obligations from God and argues that Wood has asserted a conclusion without presenting a moral model or system.
Wood's claim that killing is objectively wrong because the victim bears God's image and God grounds morality.

Dillahunty asks where God's existence entails a ban on killing, tests Wood's answer against the commanded killing of Midianites, and concludes that covenant assertions do not establish the promised foundation.
Human mortality does not erase the value of a life because its actions, relationships, and effects before death supply reasons not to kill.
The argument rebuts the claim that eventual extinction undermines secular value by identifying the foreclosed consequences and contributions caused by premature killing.
Wood's portrayal of an atheistic person as an accident headed for extinction and therefore lacking significant worth.
Dillahunty argues that focusing only on eventual death skips everything valuable between birth and death, including a person's contributions and effects on everyone connected to them.
Atheism is neither fatalism nor secular humanism, and facts about origins or extinction do not determine which proposed moral foundation is better.
The move rejects a category error central to Wood's case and restores the comparison between secular humanism and God as competing foundations for ethics.
Wood's claim that theism and atheism give morally relevant different answers about human origins, purpose, and destiny.

Dillahunty says Wood has combined atheism with psychopathy and fatalism, argues that morality concerns life before extinction, and maintains that Wood has not shown how God resolves the identified problems.
Conversion to theism can transform moral conduct by replacing a view of humans as insignificant organisms with objective obligations toward God's image-bearers.
The argument offers Wood's principal experiential evidence that a theistic foundation supplies effective restraint, objective value, and obligations absent from his former outlook.
Dillahunty's claim that Wood has not demonstrated how God fixes the foundational problems under discussion.

Wood recounts moving from violent indifference and a reductionist view of humanity to believing that persons possess God-given purpose and objective worth, with Christian commands requiring peace and concern for others.
A single conversion story shows only what motivates one individual and does not establish that God is a real or superior moral foundation.
The response directly addresses the comparative burden by separating personal motivational effectiveness from truth, general applicability, and foundational superiority.
Wood's personal conversion account offered as evidence that theism provides a better foundation for moral behavior.

Dillahunty argues that Wood's belief may be uniquely effective for Wood but lacks demonstration and general motivating force, while secular humanism openly seeks better human life through evidence, reason, and shared problem-solving.
In the absence of demonstrable cosmic justice, humans must create and enforce justice to promote a better and more compassionate society.
The move converts the absence of divine enforcement into an affirmative secular responsibility, explaining why human action is necessary for justice rather than morally futile.
Wood's objection that goal-relative morality lacks a real objective obligation or universal imperative.

Dillahunty compares morality to rule-governed evaluation, says society must intervene when people are wrong about well-being, and argues that observable injustice makes human beings the only demonstrated source of justice and aid.
Secular humanism's commitment to human justice and special human value fits a theistic image-of-God account better than an atheistic account of humans.
The move challenges whether secular humanism can ground the exceptional moral status and justice-imposing role it assigns to human beings.
Matt's claim that humans must create justice in an indifferent universe.
After Matt presents human beings as the only available agents of justice, Wood argues that this elevated role coheres with theism but not atheism.
God is unnecessary for valuing people, while secular humanism can explain why people should cooperate through broad, enlightened self-interest.
The move supplies a naturalistic motivational basis for valuing others and directly contests the claim that theism better supports human concern.
Wood's claim that atheism cannot support the special value and justice-seeking role assigned to humans.
Matt answers Wood by distinguishing secular humanism from bare atheism and arguing that cooperation and apparent altruism can arise from interests shared across society.
If enlightened selfishness is the operative motivation, wrongdoing appears permissible whenever an actor expects personal benefit and believes discovery is unlikely.
This is Wood's principal internal challenge to self-interest as a moral foundation: it allegedly cannot prohibit profitable undetected misconduct.
Matt's argument that broad-viewed self-interest can motivate altruism and produce a better social world.
Wood grants that selfishness can generate cooperative conduct, then argues that its logic changes when an individual expects to evade punishment and broader consequences.
Appealing to God does not solve opportunistic wrongdoing, because believers also expect forgiveness, while social encouragement of evasion demonstrably worsens society.
The response argues that Wood's proposed theistic alternative shares the same evasion problem and that secular norms can oppose its general adoption.
Wood's contention that self-interest permits misconduct whenever the actor expects to escape detection.
Matt argues that religious belief does not prevent people from rationalizing misconduct and shifts attention from isolated evasion to the effects of normalized behavior.
Secular humanism rejects personal exemptions and evaluates conduct by its wider effects, so undetected misconduct remains contrary to the social norms one should endorse.
The move answers the strongest evasion objection by adding causal consequences and a universal, non-exemption norm to the secular framework.
Wood's Ring-of-Gyges-style argument that selfishness cannot condemn harmless or undetectable personal wrongdoing.
Matt denies that actions are consequence-free and clarifies that selfishness was merely one route to cooperation, whereas secular humanism disallows special pleading.
Belief in God can produce morally transformative change, as illustrated by Wood's shift from violent intentions to a desire not to harm others.
The testimony supplies an experiential rebuttal to the claim that invoking God contributes nothing to resolving practical moral behavior.
Matt's repeated challenge that appealing to God solves none of Wood's objections about moral conduct.
After Matt asks how God fixes the identified problems, Wood cites his own conversion as evidence that theistic belief can substantially alter behavior.
A belief can improve conduct without being true or foundational, and an undefined God supplies neither agreed goals nor a demonstrable moral system.
The move directly compares the proposed foundations, arguing that theism's motivational effects cannot compensate for its undefined content and disputed implications.
Wood's personal testimony that belief in God transformed his violent disposition and therefore has moral force.
Matt grants that even false beliefs can motivate improvement, then argues that Wood has not derived rights, prohibitions, or shared goals from a stable account of God.
Theism makes moral intuitions reliable perceptions of objective reality, whereas naturalistic evolutionary or social explanations reduce them to useful but nonobjective dispositions.
This is a direct foundational case for theism: divine creation is said to connect moral experience to reality rather than adaptive illusion.
Matt's claim that an undefined God provides no agreed moral goals, system, or derivation of human rights.
Wood argues that humans created by a good God can treat moral intuitions as fallible but reality-directed faculties, unlike intuitions explained solely by adaptation.
Secular humanism is a demonstrable, revisable method for pursuing justice through empathy, education, discussion, and evidence, unlike an underspecified God concept.
The closing consolidates the comparative case that secular humanism has observable procedures and goals while theism lacks demonstrated properties or content.
Wood's argument that objective-seeming moral intuitions require a theistic explanation rather than natural and social causes.
Matt challenges the inference from intuition to objective obligation, then presents secular humanism as a data-responsive system for improving human life and justice.
Theism grounds objective moral obligations by explaining moral faculties as reliable products of divine creation, while atheism leaves them as wiring or social conditioning.
The closing presents Wood's fullest comparative foundation: secular goals remain conditional, whereas theism makes moral cognition truth-directed and objective.
Matt's closing claim that secular humanism is demonstrable and systematic while theism lacks usable moral content.
Wood grants that agreed goals allow instrumental rules, disputes Matt's stronger obligation claims, and argues that divine creation best explains objective moral knowledge.
God may justly end human lives, while the ancient covenant permitting harsh penalties does not authorize Christians today to kill others.
The move directly addresses whether biblical killings undermine God as a moral foundation and explains the claimed limits of their present application.
An audience question asks whether God acted morally in condoning tribal deaths, prompting a covenant-based defense and an account of Christian duties of peace.
A defense of God as morality's foundation is deficient if it avoids specifying the Christian ethical system that the defender actually invokes.
The move challenges whether an abstract theistic foundation supplies actionable ethics and whether Wood has defended the system he personally uses.
Wood's covenant-based defense of biblical killings and appeal to present Christian commands of peace.
After Wood distinguishes ancient covenant penalties from current Christian commands, Dillahunty objects that the debate shifted from generic theism toward Christianity only when concrete rules arose.
God can ground a necessary standard of goodness independently of whether Christianity is true or whether a complete Christian ethical system has been defended.
This distinction defines the pro side's principal burden by separating the metaphysical foundation of morality from a comparative defense of religious rules.
Dillahunty's objection that Wood improperly avoided defending Christianity as the concrete ethical alternative to secular humanism.
Wood answers the framing challenge by separating philosophical arguments about God's grounding role from the additional task of preparing a full comparison of ethical systems.
Objective moral facts and universal obligations require a nonphysical, humanity-transcending foundation, understood as God whose goodness is identical with being.
The move supplies the core positive argument that moral realism needs a transcendent ground and identifies that ground with divine being and goodness.
Responding to a question about the standard by which God is called good, Wood invokes privation theory, divine being, and the nonphysical character of obligations.
Defining God as goodness makes the theistic account circular and does not demonstrate that objective moral facts possess the asserted divine foundation.
This is a direct rebuttal to the pro side's metaphysical grounding argument and contests whether invoking God explains objective moral facts at all.
Wood's claim that divine being is the ground of goodness and that objective obligations require a transcendent foundation.
Immediately after Wood identifies goodness with God's being, Dillahunty argues that the account assumes rather than demonstrates an objective divine moral ground.
Secular morality is not majority rule but a fallible, revisable pursuit of better approximations to moral ideals through evidence and correction.
The move clarifies the secular humanist foundation as an improvement process capable of identifying social error rather than merely ratifying consensus.
The objection that Dillahunty's account makes majority opinion determinative of moral truth and treats exceptions as counterexamples.
An audience question asks whether ethical truth is democratic; Dillahunty cites historical moral corrections and presents current norms as tentative approximations rather than ideals.
Twentieth-century mass atrocities cannot fairly be characterized as Christian when their regimes and leaders rejected Christianity and violated Jesus's commands.
The move bears on whether historical atrocities discredit Christian morality, while conceding that such regime labels do not characterize ordinary atheists.
The audience claim that major atrocities by figures such as Hitler and Stalin should be attributed to their religious backgrounds.
Asked why notorious atrocities were committed by allegedly religious figures, Wood disputes the characterization and separates nominal Christians from Christian moral commands.
Atrocity counts by religious label are irrelevant; secular humanism rejects imposed atheism and persecution, while competing revelation claims can license violence.
The move redirects historical attribution toward guiding principles and argues that secular humanism lacks a route to killing merely over doctrinal disagreement.
Wood's emphasis on atheist regimes and his denial that atrocities associated with Hitler or nominal Christians were Christian in nature.
Dillahunty agrees that Hitler was not a secular humanist, rejects crude religious-versus-atheist atrocity accounting, and compares the operative principles behind persecution.
Secular humanism combines individual autonomy with due process and collective risk assessment, allowing proportionate intervention before or during grave threats.
The move explains how secular humanism handles dangerous actors without either absolute pacifism or unilateral vigilantism, supplying concrete decision principles.
Wood's challenge about whether intervention against a dangerous person must wait until killing begins or may occur beforehand.
After Wood probes the timing of intervention against a Hitler-like threat, Dillahunty describes historically informed due process and situation-specific proportional responses.
Human value need not be universe-wide or intrinsic because relational value, shared interests, empathy, and cooperation justify concern for everyone's flourishing.
The move provides a positive secular account of why humans should value one another without divine or intrinsic value and connects that account to cooperative flourishing.
Asked whether humans possess value in themselves or create it, Dillahunty distinguishes cosmic intrinsic value from the practical value persons have to themselves and others.
